issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere with factual findings in a second appeal only when the case involves a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court decreed a suit for specific performance on the basis of an alleged written agreement.
The first appellate court examined the evidence and found that the alleged agreement was not genuine, and that the property belonged to the defendant under a registered sale deed.
The High Court set aside the first appellate court’s findings, relying on its treatment of the alleged agreement’s scribe and of signatures on other documents, and reassessed the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had identified no substantial question of law and that its grounds concerned appreciation of evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the first appellate court’s factual findings in the second appeal. Its judgment was set aside and the first appellate court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal lies only if the case involves a substantial question of law. The High Court is expected to formulate that question and hear the appeal on it, subject to the proviso permitting consideration of another substantial question of law for recorded reasons. Reassessment of evidence, without a substantial question of law, does not justify interference with factual findings. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.

rule.if: second_appeal_from_fact_findings and high_court_reassessed_evidence and not substantial_question_of_law

predicates.second_appeal_from_fact_findings: A party brought a second appeal challenging factual findings made by the first appellate court.
predicates.high_court_reassessed_evidence: The High Court revisited or reassessed evidence to interfere with the first appellate court’s factual findings.
predicates.substantial_question_of_law: The case involved a substantial question of law warranting the High Court’s consideration in the second appeal.

issues.definition: When a High Court reexamines evidence in a second appeal from factual findings, and no substantial question of law is involved, its interference with those findings is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance cannot be decreed against a person who did not execute the alleged contract when its alleged maker had no right to dispose of the property.
material_facts: The property was conveyed to the defendant by a registered sale deed executed by other persons.
The respondent, who was a tenant of the defendant, sought specific performance against the defendant on the basis of an alleged writing made by the defendant’s mother.
The mother was not the owner of the property, and the defendant was not alleged to have executed the writing.
The sale deed did not identify the mother or the respondent as parties to the sale or indicate that it was not an outright sale.
issues.conclusion: The alleged writing could not support a decree for specific performance against the defendant, who did not execute it, where its alleged maker had no right to dispose of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance may be decreed only against the executant of the contract, provided that the executant had a right to dispose of the property. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an alleged contract concerning property.
predicates.defendant_not_contracting_executant: The person against whom specific performance was sought did not execute the alleged contract.
predicates.alleged_contract_maker_lacked_disposal_r: The person alleged to have made the contract had no right to dispose of the property.

issues.definition: In a specific performance proceeding, where the defendant did not execute the alleged contract and its alleged maker lacked the right to dispose of the property, specific performance is unenforceable against the defendant.
